opus-5.5.text:
You know, I think people often jump straight to the humanoid image, and I understand why. Our world is built for human bodies: stairs, door handles, kitchen counters, cars. So there's a real argument that a human-shaped robot can slot into that environment most easily. But I don't think humanoids will be the only form, or even the dominant one for a long time.

Look at what we already live with. A dishwasher is a robot in a sense. A Roomba is a robot. Self-driving cars are robots. Surgical systems are robots. Each takes a form dictated by the task and the environment, not by our desire to see ourselves reflected back. I expect a whole zoo of embodiments: some wheeled, some with arms mounted on counters, some small and specialized, some that you won't even recognize as robots because they're built into the walls and furniture of a home or a hospital.

What ties them together, and what I care most about, is the intelligence underneath. Regardless of form, a robot that shares space with people has to understand the 3D world: geometry, physics, where objects are, how people move, what they intend. That's spatial intelligence, and I think it's the real bottleneck, more than the hardware shape. Once machines can perceive, reason, and act in 3D space reliably, the form factor becomes almost a design choice for the use case.

And then there's the human side, which I never want us to lose sight of. When I worked on AI in healthcare, putting sensors and smart systems in hospitals and with elderly patients, the lesson was that technology has to respect human dignity, privacy, and agency. Cohabiting with robots isn't just an engineering question. Do people feel safe? Do they feel in control? Does the robot augment what a nurse or caregiver does rather than diminish them? Those questions should shape the form as much as the task does.

So my answer is diverse forms, shaped by purpose, unified by spatial intelligence, and always designed around the humans who have to live alongside them.

r001.rationale: It says robot forms should be dictated by the task and environment, and describes diverse embodiments shaped by purpose.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says humanoids will not be the only form and recommends imagining a diverse range of robot embodiments.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that there won't be one form. People tend to default to the humanoid when they picture a robot, and I understand why — we built our world for human bodies, our doors and stairs and kitchens are sized for us, so a machine shaped like us can in principle slot into that world without redesigning it. But that's an engineering argument, not a necessity, and I've always been a little skeptical of the idea that the ultimate robot looks like a person.

If you look at biology, intelligence takes an enormous range of embodiments. An octopus is extraordinarily capable with a body nothing like ours. I think robots will be similar. In a hospital you might want something that's essentially a mobile cart with very good perception and gentle manipulators. In a warehouse, arms and wheels. In a home, maybe something smaller and less imposing than a six-foot humanoid, because the form of a machine also carries a social and emotional meaning, and we underestimate that. A robot in your living room needs to be something a child and an elderly parent feel comfortable around, not just something that can open a drawer.

What I care about more than the shape is the shared foundation underneath. The reason I've spent so much time on spatial intelligence is that whatever body a robot has, it needs to understand the three-dimensional world — where objects are, how they move, what happens when you push or pour or grasp. Vision and language got us very far with the digital world, but the physical world is where humans actually live, and a machine that's going to cohabit with us has to perceive and reason about space the way we do, almost without thinking about it. Once you have that kind of general understanding, the body becomes more of a design choice fitted to the task and to the people it's with.

And I'd add one more thing: I'd like us to design these forms around human needs first. In our work at Stanford on healthcare, the question was never "what's the most impressive robot," it was "what does a nurse actually need, what does a patient actually need." When you start there, the forms you end up with are often more modest and more varied than science fiction predicts — and, I think, more useful.

r001.rationale: The response says a robot’s body is a design choice fitted to its task and the people it works with, and gives task-specific examples.

r002.rationale: It explicitly argues robots will take varied forms and describes alternatives to humanoids, such as carts, arms, and wheels.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ll see a diversity of forms, because the form should really follow the task. What do we want a robot to do, and what kind of environment does it need to operate in? A robot helping someone at home may look quite different from a robot working in a factory or helping with agriculture.

There’s a compelling argument for the humanoid form: we’ve built our environments around human bodies. Our doors, our stairs, our tools all reflect that. But that doesn’t mean every robot needs two legs and two arms. For some tasks, a simpler form could be more useful.

And cohabiting is about more than physical shape. Can the robot understand what a person is trying to do? Can it move around them safely and behave in ways they can anticipate? I think those questions are central. We should be thinking about the human experience of sharing a space with these machines, alongside what the machines are capable of doing.

r001.rationale: The response says a robot’s form should follow the task and operating environment, directly communicating task-optimized morphology.

r002.rationale: It says not every robot needs a humanoid body and that simpler forms may be more useful, endorsing forms beyond humanoids.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should be open-minded about the forms robots will take. The human form is compelling because we’ve designed our environments around our bodies—our kitchens, our tools, our doorways. But that doesn’t mean every robot needs to be humanoid. The form should follow what we want the robot to do and the environment in which it operates.

For me, the deeper question is how these machines understand and interact with the physical world, including the people in it. If a robot is helping an older person at home, being useful isn’t just about picking up an object. It’s about doing that safely, understanding what the person needs, and knowing when to ask for help. So I’m interested in a diversity of forms, but with human needs at the center of how we design them.

r001.rationale: The response says a robot’s form should follow what it is meant to do and the environment where it operates, linking morphology to its tasks.

r002.rationale: It says not every robot needs to be humanoid and expresses interest in a diversity of forms.
